title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Feeding tubes are tubes mainly inserted into the gastrointestinal tract to provide a patient with a route for enteral nutrition, though they can also be used for decompression of the gastrointestinal tract. Depending on technical and patient factors, this can be done surgically, endoscopically or by interventional radiologists. This course focuses on enteral access achieved by endoscopic placement of a feeding tube directly into the gut. Feeding tubes such as a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) and percutaneous endoscopic gastrojejunostomy (PEG-J) tubes are placed endoscopically. PEG tubes are inserted directly into the stomach, while PEG-J tubes extend into the jejunum to reduce aspiration risk in select patients- the latter is also true for jejunostomy tubes placed by surgeons and interventional radiologists. This course reviews the indications for PEG and PEG-J placement, including neurologic disorders, malignancy-related dysphagia, gastrointestinal obstruction, malnutrition, and conditions affecting cognitive or oral feeding abilities, as well as its contraindications, which range from sepsis and coagulopathy to anatomical barriers and lack of informed consent. We shall also review the techniques, complications, as well as methods to replace gastrostomy tubes.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: With this course, participants will gain an understanding of patient selection and procedural techniques for PEG and PEG-J tube placements, which are essential for optimal interprofessional care. Postprocedure care, including recognition and management of complications, eg, infection, tube dislodgement, buried bumper syndrome, and aspiration, is also discussed. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in performing PEG and PEG-J procedures, applying recommended techniques, preventing complications, performing gastrostomy tube replacement, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach to improve patient outcomes.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify appropriate patients for percutaneous gastrostomy and jejunostomy placement based on clinical indications. Apply evidence-based procedural techniques to optimize technical success in the placement of percutaneous gastrostomy and jejunostomy tubes. Assess patient risk factors for procedure-related adverse events associated with percutaneous gastrostomy and jejunostomy procedures. Collaborate with interprofessional team members to improve care coordination and outcomes in patients undergoing percutaneous gastrostomy and jejunostomy procedures. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Introduction
content: Feeding tubes are tubes inserted into the gastrointestinal tract to provide a route for enteral nutrition, though they can also be used for decompression of the gastrointestinal tract. Tubes come in a variety of sizes, lengths, and materials, depending on their longevity, placement method, and location. Among feeding tubes, percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) and percutaneous endoscopic gastrojejunostomy (PEG-J) tube placement are widely performed procedures for long-term enteral nutritional support. These techniques offer minimally invasive alternatives to nasoenteric feeding and surgically placed feeding tubes via laparotomy. First introduced in 1980, PEG tube placement demonstrates a technical success rate exceeding 95%. The procedure is typically performed under moderate sedation, with an estimated procedure-related mortality of approximately 0.5%.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Introduction
content: PEG and PEG-J tubes play a critical role in patients who are unable to maintain adequate oral intake due to a variety of conditions. These include benign and malignant obstructive processes, iatrogenic causes such as radiation-induced esophageal injury leading to mechanical obstruction, esophageal motility disorders, and neurologic conditions resulting in oropharyngeal dysphagia. Additional indications include cognitive and psychosocial disorders, such as dementia, as well as developmental disabilities that impair safe and effective oral feeding.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Introduction
content: In PEG tube placement, a tube is inserted directly into the stomach through the abdominal wall. In PEG-J tube placement, an extension is placed via the existing PEG tube into the jejunum to allow jejunal feeding. The latter is particularly useful in patients at high risk of aspiration from gastric feedings, eg, those with gastroparesis, gastric outlet obstruction, severe gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), gastric resection, a history of repeated aspiration, or who cannot tolerate gastric feeding. The placement of a PEG-J tube, however, has not been shown to prevent aspiration. [1] [2] [3] [4]

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Introduction
content: Once the PEG tube is placed, a fistulous gastrocutaneous tract forms in approximately 2 to 4 weeks, although this may be delayed in patients with severe malnutrition, immunocompromised patients, or significant ascites. If a PEG tube is dislodged within a month after placement when the tract isn't mature, then endoscopic replacement is recommended. Otherwise, bedside replacement is usually sufficient. If the tube is dislodged within 4 weeks of initial placement, patients are at significant risk of peritonitis and perforation due to peritoneal spillage of gastric contents through the immature track, and replacement should not be attempted without expert consultation. A blind attempt to reinsert the tube or even a Foley placement in an immature tract can lead to inadvertent placement of the tube into the peritoneal cavity. Replacement of a PEG-J tube requires either endoscopic guidance with or without fluoroscopy or interventional radiology.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Before placing a percutaneous or open gastrostomy tube, reviewing the anatomy of the stomach and surrounding areas is important. The stomach is divided into different anatomical parts. The gastroesophageal junction is the point at which the esophagus meets the stomach. The fundus of the stomach is the superior portion lying closest to the diaphragm. The pylorus is the valve that leads out of the stomach into the duodenum. Next to the pylorus is the antrum, and the remainder of the stomach is called the body. Ideally, a feeding tube is placed in the anterior wall of the body of the stomach.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Attached to the greater curvature is the greater omentum, which forms the gastrocolic ligament and connects to the transverse colon. The proximity of the stomach to the transverse colon should be considered, especially during placement of a percutaneous gastrostomy tube.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Not only is normal anatomy essential, but clinicians should also consider variants of normal. A person with hepatomegaly may have a left lobe of the liver that crosses past the midline. Though preoperative imaging is not needed, if prior imaging is available, it should be reviewed before performing a feeding tube procedure. In addition, reviewing the patient’s surgical history and performing a thorough abdominal inspection are imperative.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Indications
content: Feeding tube placement is indicated when a mismatch between calorie intake and metabolic demands is present. For patients with poor oral intake for 5 to 7 days and requiring long-term nutritional support for more than 30 days, enteral feeding access should be initiated within 24 to 48 hours of admission. [5] [6] [1] Before placement of a feeding tube, addressing the anticipated duration of enteral nutrition, the patient's life expectancy, treatment goals, diagnosis, and ethical preferences is important. If a patient will only need enteral nutrition for a short period or the duration is unknown, a temporary feeding tube may be placed. This is most commonly used to provide enteral nutrition to patients who require intubation and mechanical ventilation and therefore cannot swallow. This tube is most commonly an 8 to 12 French flexible tube inserted orally or via a nare with the tip ending in the stomach or jejunum. The location of the distal tip is most commonly confirmed with plain film x-ray.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Indications
content: Dislodged PEG tube: If the tube is dislodged within 24 hours, a temporary tube (eg, Foley catheter) should be placed in the track to prevent track closure, which begins anytime between 8 and 24 hours and narrows further over time. Malfunctioning PEG tube Obstructed G-tube not responding to traditional unclogging measures (eg, flushing with water or pancreatic enzymes mixed with bicarbonate solution)

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Contraindications
content: Medical necessity must be confirmed before performing the procedure. However, contraindications for PEG and PEG-J tube placement fall into 2 categories: absolute and relative. [10] Absolute contraindications include: Sepsis Hemodynamic instability Severe ascites Peritonitis Coagulopathy (international normalized ratio (INR) greater than 1.5 or a platelet count of less than 50,000/uL) Abdominal wall infection at the site of insertion Gastric outlet obstruction and severe gastroparesis (if used for feeding) Interposed organs (the colon is the most common organ) Total gastrectomy Lack of informed consent for the procedure Failure to apposition the anterior gastric wall to the abdominal wall Relative contraindications include: Obesity (might hinder transillumination during the procedure and finding the appropriate site on the abdominal wall) Presence of nonobstructive oropharyngeal or esophageal malignancy Hepatomegaly Splenomegaly Peritoneal dialysis Gastric varices Partial gastrectomy

content: For bedside or blind PEG tube replacement, contraindications include: G-tube displacement or malfunction within 4 weeks of initial tube placement (due to track immaturity) [11] Massive ascites Any signs of peritonitis Coagulation disorders The tube has been displaced for more than 24 hours, and the track has narrowed or closed

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Equipment
content: Several commercially available kits and variations in techniques have been introduced. In a gastroenterology practice, an endoscope is needed for transillumination and for performing the procedure. Generally, the PEG tube kit includes: A silicone tube (eg, high-grade silicone dome-bolstered PEG tube) Universal retrieval snare Tray packaging to improve the efficiency of the procedure External bolsters Radiologic placement of PEG and PEG-J tubes can differ slightly and does not require an endoscope. For bedside replacement of G-tube, equipment that is generally needed includes: G-tube (size similar to prior G-tube) 10 mL saline syringe Guidewire Dressing kit 2 x 2 and 4 x 4 gauze Alcohol swabs and povidone-iodine swabs For endoscopic replacement of the G-tube, the equipment needed is similar to that for placing a new tube.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Personnel
content: A gastroenterologist or endoscopist, a second operator, and support staff, including a nurse, are needed to perform the procedure. While this procedure is typically performed with moderate sedation, an anesthesiologist is usually present when monitored anesthesia care is the recommended type of sedation for certain patients. However, when these tubes are placed by the radiology team, a gastroenterologist or endoscopist is not present.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Preparation
content: Placing a feeding tube is usually an elective procedure. In surgical cases, a few instances may arise in which a surgeon chooses to place a feeding tube concurrently with an emergent procedure if long-term tube feeding is anticipated, though this is not the norm.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Preparation
content: Informed consent must be obtained from the patient or their legal representative before the procedure. Additionally, patients should fast overnight for approximately 8 hours and receive prophylactic intravenous antibiotics 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure. [12] [13]

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Preparation
content: The American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE) and the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) recommend continuing antiplatelet therapy during PEG tube placement, as current evidence does not indicate a significant increase in bleeding risk. Anticoagulant therapy, however, requires a risk-benefit assessment, particularly for patients at high thrombotic risk. Interprofessional discussion should guide decisions regarding holding anticoagulants before the procedure if clinically appropriate. [14] [15] [7]

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Preparation
content: Antibiotic regimens should be selected based on methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) status. Patients testing negative for MRSA or at low MRSA risk should receive intravenous (IV) cefazolin 2 g for patients weighing less than 120 kg or 3 g IV for patients weighing 120 kg or more. Clindamycin 900 mg IV is preferred for patients with penicillin or cephalosporin hypersensitivity. If the procedure is prolonged, a second dose of cefazolin should be administered 4 hours after the first, or 6 hours after the initial dose of clindamycin. Patients testing positive for MRSA or considered at high MRSA risk should undergo decontamination if feasible. Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV, up to a maximum of 2 g, should be infused over 60 to 90 minutes, starting within 120 minutes before the surgical incision. Redosing is not required for prolonged procedures.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Preparation
content: For bedside replacement of the PEG tube, first, if the tube is still in place, it should be examined. Taking careful history and reviewing prior records, when available, is vital to determine the type of tube that has been placed (an internal mushroom cap versus an internal balloon). The dressing is removed, and the percutaneous incision site is examined for signs of infection, track closure, or subcutaneous tissue displacement. The area should be appropriately cleaned with a sterilizing agent, such as alcohol or povidone-iodine. The area is covered with either the sheath from the PEG replacement kit or surgical drapes to prevent contamination of the surroundings during PEG replacement.

content: Several different techniques have been developed for PEG tube insertion. title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Technique or Treatment -- Pull Technique (Ponsky Technique)
content: The "pull" technique is most commonly used and was initially described by Gauderer et al. A string is attached to a needle, which is inserted through the abdominal wall into the stomach. This string is grasped with endoscopic biopsy forceps or a snare, and then the endoscope is retracted, taking out the string through the esophagus and mouth. Then the string is attached to the external end of the PEG tube and pulled back through the abdominal wall. This results in removing the tube from the mouth, through the esophagus and stomach, and then out of the body through the abdominal wall. [16]

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Technique or Treatment -- Push Technique (Sacks-Vine Technique)
content: In the "push" technique, a guidewire is inserted into the stomach, as in the pull technique, and retrieved through the mouth as the endoscope is withdrawn. The feeding tube, with the external end leading, is then advanced over the guidewire, passes into the stomach, and exits through the puncture site. [17] Introducer Technique (Russell Technique)

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Technique or Treatment -- Push Technique (Sacks-Vine Technique)
content: The introducer, or Russell, technique utilizes the Seldinger method. Under endoscopic visualization, a guidewire is placed into the stomach, followed by advancement of a dilating catheter and sheath over the guidewire. After removing the guidewire, the PEG tube is introduced through the peel-away sheath. Numerous instructional videos are available online, and those published by national medical societies are recommended for guidance.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Technique or Treatment -- Imaging Guidance
content: Percutaneous transabdominal gastrostomy can be performed using either radiographic imaging or endoscopic guidance. In patients with head and neck malignancies, upper gastrointestinal obstruction, or strictures, the safe track method is advised to prevent bowel injury during transabdominal percutaneous gastrostomy. [18]
contents: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Technique or Treatment -- Imaging Guidance. Percutaneous transabdominal gastrostomy can be performed using either radiographic imaging or endoscopic guidance. In patients with head and neck malignancies, upper gastrointestinal obstruction, or strictures, the safe track method is advised to prevent bowel injury during transabdominal percutaneous gastrostomy. [18]

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Technique or Treatment -- Imaging Guidance
content: Additional techniques include ultrasound-guided percutaneous gastrostomy (PUG), which offers a safe alternative to fluoroscopy-guided placement (PRG), particularly in critically ill patients. PUG eliminates radiation exposure without increasing the risk of complications. [19] Studies of balloon and bumper-type tubes demonstrate low complication rates, although balloon tubes have been associated with increased hospital readmissions and extended stays exceeding 24 hours postprocedure. [20] Larger-caliber direct percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy (DPEJ) tubes, compared with PEG-J tubes, provide longer patency and require fewer reinterventions, but they frequently result in periostomal leakage. [21] [22]

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Technique or Treatment -- PEG Tube Replacement
content: If the PEG tube is not completely dislodged but is clogged or malfunctioning, the old tube must be removed. If the old tube is an endoscopically placed tube with an internal mushroom tip, then gentle traction is applied to the external portion of the tube to remove the internal mushroom, as excessive force can disrupt even a well-formed track. If the old G-tube has an internal balloon, the balloon is deflated by aspirating fluid through the balloon port, typically 8 to 10 mL, and the tube is removed.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Technique or Treatment -- PEG Tube Replacement
content: For a replacement G-tube, balloon-tip tubes with a similar diameter to the prior tube should be used as a replacement. First, the balloon's functioning should be confirmed. Then, the balloon tip G-tube is either inserted blindly into the track or advanced with a guidewire, with or without fluoroscopy. Once fully inside, the balloon is inflated with 8 to 10 mL of saline or distilled water, and the tube is slowly retracted until gentle resistance is encountered, as the balloon opposes the gastric wall. The external portion of the tube is secured with a dressing. Both ports of a traditional G-tube (the feeding port and the med port) are flushed, then capped. A dressing is then applied in accordance with institutional policy.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Complications
content: PEG tube insertion is widely regarded as a safe and effective procedure, with technical success rates exceeding 95%. Nevertheless, procedure-related complications may occur. Although most studies report low procedure-related mortality, this risk is higher among patients with significant underlying comorbid conditions. [23] PEG tube placement has been associated with fewer inpatient adverse events compared with gastrostomy tubes placed via interventional radiology or surgical approaches. [24] Complication rates specific to PEG-J have not been independently well characterized but are generally considered comparable to those observed with PEG tube placement.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Complications
content: Overall, complication rates secondary to any cause at 30 days post-PEG tube placement range from 4.8% to 15%. Major complications account for 0.2% to 3% of cases, while minor complications account for 11% to 16%. [25] [26] [27] In the intensive care unit setting, patients requiring PEG or percutaneous radiologic/interventional radiology–guided gastrostomy (PRG/IRG) tubes exhibited an overall complication rate of 22.3%, with tube dysfunction and dislodgement representing the most frequent adverse events. Major complications necessitating operative or procedural intervention occurred in 11.2% of cases. Patients undergoing PRG/IRG placement demonstrated higher rates of both all-cause and major complications compared with those receiving PEG tubes. [28] Two studies showed that IRG was associated with significantly higher complication rates related to bleeding and colon perforation. [27] [29] [30] [24]

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Complications
content: All-cause mortality following PEG tube placement varies across study populations and clinical indications. Reported mortality rates may reach approximately 15% at 30 days and up to 28% at 90 days among patients with neurologic disorders. PEG tube placement for malignancy has also been associated with higher mortality. Additionally, several patient-related factors have been identified as predictors of increased mortality, including diabetes mellitus, elevated C-reactive protein levels, female sex, advanced age, heart failure, and lower body mass index. [25]

content: Major complications of PEG and PEG-J tube placement include: Hemorrhage Aspiration pneumonia Buried bumper syndrome Necrotizing fasciitis Perforation of bowel Metastatic seeding

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Complications -- Major Complications
content: Hemorrhage involves bleeding from the PEG tract, gastric artery, mesenteric or splenic vein injuries, and rectus sheath hematoma. [32] [33] While applying pressure over the abdominal wall might be sufficient for mild cases, endoscopic or surgical exploration may be required in select cases. Furthermore, aspiration pneumonia is a serious as well as a potentially fatal complication associated with PEG tube feeding, with its risk increasing with high-volume feeding and the prone position. [34]

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Complications -- Major Complications
content: Buried bumper syndrome occurs when excessive tension develops between the external and internal bumpers, causing ischemic necrosis of the gastric wall. This may lead to migration of the PEG tube towards the abdominal wall. As a result, the tube may dislodge, leading to peristomal leakage, feeding difficulties, and swelling and pain at the insertion site. [35] The tube should be removed as soon as the diagnosis is made to avoid serious complications, eg, peritonitis and gastric perforation.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Complications -- Major Complications
content: Necrotizing fasciitis is very rare with PEG and PEG-J tubes; however, pressure or traction on the PEG tube increases its risk. Keeping the external bumper 1 to 2 cm away from the abdomen may help prevent this complication. Necrotizing fasciitis is an acute surgical emergency and requires broad-spectrum antibiotics, intensive care support, and surgical debridement.

content: Any intra-abdominal organ is at risk of injury during PEG tube placement. Diagnosis can be challenging since most patients who require PEG tubes are often unable to communicate abdominal discomfort. Hemodynamic instability should prompt a thorough investigation, and a computed tomography scan (CT) of the abdomen with water-soluble enteric contrast or fluoroscopy may be useful.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Complications -- Minor Complications
content: Infection at the tube site represents the most common minor complication following PEG tube placement. Signs may include redness around the stoma and purulent drainage. Topical antibiotics are sufficient for mild cases, while severe infections require thorough evaluation and appropriate medical or surgical management. Peristomal leakage occurs more frequently in debilitated patients and warrants careful assessment to rule out additional complications. When necessary, the PEG tube should be removed, the tract allowed to heal completely, and a new tube placed if medically indicated.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Complications -- Minor Complications
content: Tube dislodgement can be managed differently depending on tract maturity. If the tract has matured, blind replacement without endoscopy is possible. In cases of uncertainty, instillation of a water-soluble contrast through the PEG tube helps confirm proper positioning.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Complications -- Minor Complications
content: Gastric outlet obstruction is uncommon and arises when the tube migrates into the pyloric region. Computed tomography of the abdomen can confirm tube position, and maintaining the external bumper 1 to 2 cm from the abdominal wall reduces this risk. Pneumoperitoneum occurs frequently after PEG insertion due to abdominal insufflation during the procedure. Persistence of free air beyond 72 hours or the presence of peritoneal signs should trigger further evaluation.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Complications -- Minor Complications
content: Tube blockage is most common with small-bore feeding tubes and may result from thick formulas, improperly crushed medications, or incompatibilities between medications and enteral feeds. Management strategies include attaching a 50 mL syringe filled with warm water for a pull-and-push technique, gently squeezing the tube, or mixing pancreatic enzymes with a bicarbonate solution before flushing with warm water. [41]

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Complications -- PEG Replacement
content: The major complication of PEG tube replacement is accidental peritoneal placement. This should be suspected when the patient starts having abdominal pain, fever, and signs of frank peritonitis on the exam. A prompt investigation should be performed using a contrast-enhanced x-ray or a computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen. Tube feeds should be stopped immediately. A surgical consultation should be obtained, and broad-spectrum antibiotics should be initiated promptly. The patient is then managed conservatively with close hemodynamic monitoring, with surgical assistance as indicated.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Clinical Significance
content: Placement of a PEG or PEG-J tube is a common procedure with numerous indications. Hence, clinicians and support staff should be aware of its indications, contraindications, and complications. PEG and PEG-J tube placement holds significant clinical importance for patients requiring long-term enteral nutrition due to impaired oral intake from neurologic disorders, malignancy-related dysphagia, gastrointestinal obstruction, or chronic medical conditions. By providing a safe, minimally invasive route for nutritional support, PEG tubes improve caloric delivery, reduce the risk of malnutrition, and support overall patient outcomes. Proper patient selection, adherence to procedural protocols, and management of potential complications—including infection, tube dislodgement, peristomal leakage, gastric outlet obstruction, and tube blockage—are essential to optimizing safety and effectiveness. PEG-J and DPEJ extensions further expand clinical utility by addressing high aspiration risk and enhancing feeding tolerance in complex cases, while interprofessional collaboration ensures coordinated care and long-term monitoring, reinforcing both patient safety and nutritional success.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Clinical Significance
content: G-tube malfunction is commonly encountered in clinical practice, both in inpatient and outpatient settings. If the patient is seen in the clinic, emergency department, or a nursing home for a malfunctioning G-tube, an appropriate service, either gastroenterology or interventional radiology, should be consulted. The longer the tube has been out of place, the higher the chance that the track has narrowed or closed. If more than 24 hours have elapsed since the G-tube was displaced, a blind, forceful attempt to insert a Foley or G-tube should not be performed, and replacement should be referred to specialized services (gastrointestinal or interventional radiology).

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: PEG and PEG-J tubes provide safe, minimally invasive methods for delivering long-term enteral nutrition to patients who cannot maintain adequate oral intake due to neurologic, oncologic, or gastrointestinal conditions. These procedures offer reliable access for nutritional support and medication administration while reducing the need for nasoenteric or surgically placed feeding tubes. Proper patient selection, adherence to procedural protocols, and vigilant post-procedure monitoring are critical to minimizing complications such as infection, tube dislodgement, peristomal leakage, gastric outlet obstruction, and tube blockage. Pre-procedural assessment, including informed consent and review of comorbidities, anticoagulant status, and antibiotic prophylaxis, enhances safety and aligns care with the patient’s medical needs and personal preferences.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective management of PEG and PEG-J tubes requires coordinated interprofessional collaboration. Physicians, advanced practitioners, and general practitioners are responsible for evaluating indications, performing or overseeing procedures, and promptly addressing complications. Nurses provide direct patient care, monitor tube function, and educate patients and families on tube maintenance and feeding techniques. Pharmacists contribute by reviewing medication compatibility with enteral feeds and recommending safe administration strategies. Dietitians and other health professionals develop individualized nutrition plans, while the broader care team engages in clear communication regarding goals of care, procedural expectations, and patient preferences. Through collaborative planning, skillful execution, and ongoing monitoring, the team enhances patient-centered outcomes, improves safety, and ensures that interventions align with the patient’s quality-of-life goals, particularly in populations with limited prognosis or complex comorbidities. [44] [45] For PEG tube replacement, a discussion should be had regarding the continued need for the PEG tube. Replacement should be performed with expert consultation.

title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: The PEG tract typically requires approximately 4 weeks to mature. Once enteral access is no longer clinically indicated, the PEG tube may be removed. The technique for removal depends on the specific type of PEG tube in place. If the tube type cannot be reliably identified or if there is concern about potential complications during removal, removal under upper endoscopic guidance is recommended. Following tube removal, the site should be cleansed, covered with sterile gauze, and appropriately monitored.

If unsuccessful or the tube gets dislodged, expert consultation is recommended.

Once the tract has fully healed, routine tube care should include daily rotation of the tube by approximately 180 degrees and gentle in-and-out movement of 1 to 2 cm to maintain tract patency and prevent tissue overgrowth.
